a5647.speaker: Philippe Lazzarini, commissioner-general of UNRWA
a5647.name: Philippe Lazzarini
a5647.title: commissioner-general of UNRWA
a5647.speech: Has warned that the situation in Gaza is “deteriorating very, very quickly”, more than a week after Israel again halted all supplies from entering the Gaza Strip: “Whatever the intent is, it’s clearly a weaponisation of humanitarian aid into Gaza” ; “It is critical that humanitarian aid is allowed into Gaza again to maintain the progress made during the first phase of the ceasefire and meet people’s basic needs,” adding that there remains a risk of returning to the “deepening hunger” seen before the recent ceasefire.

a5647.speaker: Philippe Lazzarini, commissioner-general of UNRWA
a5647.name: Philippe Lazzarini
a5647.title: commissioner-general of UNRWA
a5647.speech: Has repeatedly said the agency could only be replaced by “capable Palestinian institutions” within “a Palestinian state”, amid his agency being banned by the Israeli government.

a5647.speaker: Philippe Lazzarini, commissioner-general of UNRWA
a5647.name: Philippe Lazzarini
a5647.title: commissioner-general of UNRWA
a5647.speech: Told journalists that “a fierce disinformation campaign”, legislation outlawing UNRWA in Israel’s parliament and “the suspension of funding by key donors” have taken a toll on the agency; warned that UNRWA cannot be allowed to “implode”: “Collapse would create a dangerous vacuum in the occupied Palestinian territory and send shockwaves through Jordan, Lebanon and Syria” ; “An environment in which children are deprived of education, and people lack access to basic services, is fertile ground for exploitation and extremism” ; added that the agency’s financial situation is also “critical and precarious”.

a5647.speaker: AFP
a5647.name: AFP
a5647.speech: Reported on Monday that Germany said Israel’s decision to halt aid deliveries and cut off the electricity supply to Gaza could prompt a fresh humanitarian crisis in the Palestinian territory.

a5647.speaker: Kathrin Deschauer, German foreign ministry spokesperson
a5647.name: Kathrin Deschauer
a5647.title: German foreign ministry spokesperson
a5647.speech: Told a regular press conference that Gaza was “again threatened with a food shortage” ; “We note with great concern the cutting off of electricity and the discussion about stopping the water supply” ; “Such steps are or would be unacceptable and incompatible with (Israel’s) obligations under international law.”

a5647.speaker: The Times of Israel
a5647.name: The Times of Israel
a5647.speech: According to it, US funding for Gaza’s relief efforts may have been caught up in the Trump administration’s sweeping cuts to the US Agency for International Development (USAID).

a5647.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State (post on X)
a5647.name: Marco Rubio
a5647.title: US Secretary of State (post on X)
a5647.speech: Wrote that “after a 6 week review we are officially cancelling 83% of the programmes at USAID.”

a5647.speaker: Trump administration
a5647.name: Trump administration
a5647.speech: Had initially said that the only exceptions to the cuts would be aid programmes in Israel and Egypt.

a5647.speaker: US State Department
a5647.name: US State Department
a5647.speech: According to it, Rubio discussed Gaza reconstruction efforts with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Monday.

a5647.speaker: Hamas
a5647.name: Hamas
a5647.speech: Said on Monday that Israel has also failed to live up to its side of the agreement by refusing to withdraw its troops from the Philadelphi Corridor and preventing outside aid from reaching Gaza directly.

a5768.speaker: BBC Media Action 2024 report
a5768.name: BBC Media Action 2024 report
a5768.speech: According to a 2024 report, USAID donated $3.23m (£2.6m) to BBC Media Action, making it the charity’s second-largest donor that financial year

a5768.speaker: US government data
a5768.name: US government data
a5768.speech: According to government data, the US spent $68bn (£55bn) on international aid in 2023, of which USAID’s budget constitutes more than half at around $40bn

a5768.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5768.name: Donald Trump
a5768.title: US President
a5768.speech: Is a long-term critic of overseas spending and has said it does not represent value for money for American taxpayers; has singled out USAID for particularly strong criticism, describing senior officials there as “radical lunatics” ; has made it clear he wants overseas spending to be closely aligned with his “America First” approach

a5768.speaker: Chicago Council on Global Affairs
a5768.name: Chicago Council on Global Affairs
a5768.speech: According to the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, polling data going back to the 1970s has indicated broad support for cuts to foreign aid spending

a5768.speaker: US State Department (memo)
a5768.name: US State Department (memo)
a5768.speech: A memo was issued by the State Department which halted the vast majority of work being done on the ground; waivers were later issued for humanitarian programmes

a5768.speaker: One veteran humanitarian worker (anonymous)
a5768.name: One veteran humanitarian worker (anonymous)
a5768.speech: Told the BBC the pause was “like an earthquake across the aid sector”

a5768.speaker: Elon Musk, adviser to President Trump
a5768.name: Elon Musk
a5768.title: adviser to President Trump
a5768.speech: Speaking in a public conversation on X, the social media platform he owns, said: “With regards to the USAID stuff, I went over it with [the president] in detail and he agreed that we should shut it down.”

a5768.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a5768.name: Marco Rubio
a5768.title: US Secretary of State
a5768.speech: Accused USAID’s leadership of “insubordination” and said he was now its “acting head”; added that “a lot of functions” carried out by the agency would continue but that spending “has to be in alignment with the national interest”

a5768.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a5768.name: Marco Rubio
a5768.title: US Secretary of State
a5768.speech: After the 90-day overseas spending freeze was announced, said “every dollar” must be “justified” by evidence that it makes the US safer, stronger and more prosperous

a5768.speaker: UK Ministers (2020, on the merger of the Department for International Development with the Foreign Office)
a5768.name: UK Ministers (2020
a5768.title: on the merger of the Department for International Development with the Foreign Office)
a5768.speech: Said at the time that it would ensure international spending supported the government’s wider foreign policy goals

a5925.speaker: Maritza Chan Valverde, Ambassador of Costa Rica to the UN (co-chair of the Conference)
a5925.name: Maritza Chan Valverde
a5925.title: Ambassador of Costa Rica to the UN (co-chair of the Conference)
a5925.speech: Indicated that “1,500 delegates, 195 countries, 500 binding commitments and 100 billion dollars in new financing” are expected, as well as “historic maximum results” ; “The third United Nations Ocean Conference (UNOC3) will reverse the decline of the Oceans by 2030 or will document humanity's failure to act. Five days, one ocean, one unique opportunity” ; without going into great detail about the entities and actors that will provide that financing, stated that during UNOC3's Blue Economy Finance Forum, Wall Street executives will commit to “50 billion dollars (44.11 billion euros) in sustainable ocean investments and the creation of 10 million blue-economy jobs by 2030”.

a5925.speaker: Jérôme Bonnafont, French Ambassador to the UN
a5925.name: Jérôme Bonnafont
a5925.title: French Ambassador to the UN
a5925.speech: Refused to say where the financing will come from, stressing that the announcements will be made in the course of the conference, but guaranteed that he “expects many resources that will reaffirm the commitments to the Ocean”; stated that France's objective with the Nice conference is to “produce an agreement that is pro-oceans, as the Paris agreement of 10 years ago was for the climate”.

a5925.speaker: Jérôme Bonnafont, French Ambassador to the UN
a5925.name: Jérôme Bonnafont
a5925.title: French Ambassador to the UN
a5925.speech: “It is our ambition to ensure that this treaty, which showed us the urgency of this matter a few weeks ago, enters into force. (...) It is really important that this treaty becomes international law throughout the world” (on ratification of the High Seas Treaty / BBNJ).

a5925.speaker: Li Junhua, UN Under-Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs
a5925.name: Li Junhua
a5925.title: UN Under-Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs
a5925.speech: Assured that UNOC3 “will not be just another routine meeting” and stated that the future of the ocean will be shaped by the decisions and actions taken now.

a5925.speaker: Organisers of UNOC3
a5925.name: Organisers of UNOC3
a5925.speech: Indicated that, although Washington has not indicated that it will take part in the event, “many North American cities, companies and scientists” will be present in Nice ; stressed that the risk “of seeing the oceans become spaces for uncontrolled competition for the exploitation of natural resources” is one of the reasons for “working so actively to secure the ratification of the BBNJ”.

a6140.speaker: Mrs Anjor Obande, Founder of the JorJor Mother and Child Foundation
a6140.name: Mrs Anjor Obande
a6140.title: Founder of the JorJor Mother and Child Foundation
a6140.speech: Has called on Nigerians to extend support to vulnerable citizens struggling to access basic necessities, including food ; speaking at the event, she emphasized the growing need for humanitarian assistance, particularly for individuals and families facing severe economic hardships ; “The current economic hardship is taking a toll on many families, leaving countless parents unable to provide even a single meal for their children. This is why we are here today, to bring relief and support to as many families as we can. That’s the essence of this programme. Our goal is to reach as many communities as possible. We chose to start with Mpape, and from here, we plan to extend our outreach to other states across Nigeria. This is our commitment to doing our part in alleviating the burden on families during these trying times.” ; “Today, we extended support to over 100 families by distributing essential items. Each family received a bag of rice, cartons of noodles and spaghetti, as well as packs of seasoning cubes, tomato paste, and cash assistance. Passersby were not left out, as we ensured they also benefited from the outreach. A bag of rice can sustain a family of four, five, or even six for a while, providing some reassurance that they will have food at home. This initiative reflects our commitment to making a meaningful difference in the lives of those in need.”

a6140.speaker: JorJor Mother and Child Foundation (statement)
a6140.name: JorJor Mother and Child Foundation (statement)
a6140.speech: In a statement, the foundation stressed the increasing struggles faced by families due to the prevailing economic challenges. Many individuals are finding it increasingly difficult to afford basic needs, including food and other essentials for their families.

a6140.speaker: Mrs Franca Odu, beneficiary of the initiative, a mother of two
a6140.name: Mrs Franca Odu
a6140.title: beneficiary of the initiative, a mother of two
a6140.speech: Expressed her gratitude and joy at receiving support from the foundation: “I am so happy to benefit from this kind gesture. This is the first time I am receiving this kind of assistance. I have lived here for 17 years, paying revenue and other dues, yet I have not encountered individuals like this who offer help without regard to religion or tribe.” ; “The benefactor came, saw women, widows, ageing mothers, and the less privileged, and chose to help us out of her good heart. She brought bags of rice, packs of spaghetti and noodles, seasonings, tomatoes, and even sanitary pads. It was such a thoughtful and life-changing intervention.”

a6140.speaker: Mrs Franca Odu, beneficiary of the initiative, a mother of two
a6140.name: Mrs Franca Odu
a6140.title: beneficiary of the initiative, a mother of two
a6140.speech: Appealed to other well-meaning Nigerians to emulate the foundation’s gesture: “I want to seize this opportunity to beg well-meaning Nigerians to please emulate this foundation. People are really suffering because there is hunger in the land.”

a6140.speaker: An observer (anonymous)
a6140.name: An observer (anonymous)
a6140.speech: “She planned for a specific number of people, but the turnout was far beyond her expectations. Without hesitation, she went to her car, retrieved a bundle of cash, and distributed it among those who couldn’t receive the items, ensuring no one left empty-handed,” an observer recounted.

a6140.speaker: One of the beneficiaries (unnamed)
a6140.name: One of the beneficiaries (unnamed)
a6140.speech: Offered heartfelt prayers: “May God continue to bless her abundantly. Wherever she gets the resources to provide all these items and reach out to us, may God replenish her pockets. I pray for more promotion and favor in her life, in Jesus’ name.”

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: "The goal and vision of this administration's foreign policy, President Trump's second, is to put the United States first: America First. This means that every dollar we spend, every programme we fund and every policy adopted must be justified by its contribution to making the United States safer, stronger and more prosperous. So we are evaluating our work abroad always with that vision and that goal in mind."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On immigration: "The objective of President Trump and his administration is to contain mass migration and protect the borders. That is why we are giving priority to protecting our borders in order to halt illegal migration, which is also a destabilising factor, and to working with other countries to negotiate the repatriation of illegal immigrants. It is the responsibility of every nation to readmit its citizens who are in the United States illegally." ; "The priority is whoever has committed a crime, but the details of the deportation process are handled by the Department of Homeland Security... we are working with all countries in the world, including in Africa, so that they receive the citizens who will now return to their countries... without security there can be no prosperity... when countries have strong economies and job opportunities, people do not feel pressure to emigrate." ; "Of course, because everything is interconnected... migrating illegally is extremely dangerous... The only people who benefit from mass illegal migration are the traffickers." ; On airport borders: "the Department of Homeland Security... is the one that can speak about the details... for President Trump's administration the security of the United States is a high priority, so everything that has to do with our immigration system is being strengthened, with more resources, more work and more attention."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On the USAID suspension: "The administration decided to make a 90-day pause in foreign aid. The purpose of this pause is to evaluate and ensure that all United States programmes and initiatives abroad are aligned with the country's interests. The definition of 'humanitarian' has expanded too much... It is important to stress that there is a waiver process for life-saving humanitarian assistance during this review period. This measure is temporary and provides for limited exceptions... This pause does not mean that the United States will stop offering humanitarian assistance. No. The administration decided that a realignment is necessary, because this money comes from the taxes of American citizens... it is very important to ensure that this money, which is the money of the American people, is being spent in the most effective way possible, with the greatest results."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On the Millennium Challenge Corporation compacts: "The Millennium Challenge Corporation is an example of a global initiative that we carry out in partnership with many other countries. At this moment, we are also evaluating whether we are going to continue to be part of these initiatives and in what way we are going to offer aid. I would say it is part of this evaluation process that we are carrying out."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On what the aid suspension means for Africa: "The United States has this policy of putting the country first. But that does not mean that we are going to work alone, in isolation. We are going to continue to seek and develop partnerships with other countries, with the private sector, in all parts of the world, including in Africa. We understand that Africa has many resources and many opportunities; it also has a large, young population with a great deal to offer... always having as a goal the objective of making the United States safer, more prosperous and stronger... putting the United States first does not mean that the United States will not work with other countries."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On protectionism and China: "We understand that, in Africa and in other parts of the world, as our regional partners grow stronger, they can more easily resist countries such as China, which often promise a lot but deliver little... in China, there is no divergence between commercial and political interests. State enterprises are controlled by the State, for the good of the State. It is each country's decision to decide which other countries it will work with, but there are some real risks in working with China. Chinese influence is real and represents not only a threat to the national security of the United States, but to other countries as well."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On AGOA and trade initiatives: "The administration is still very young. It is still determining which economic initiatives it will propose in the different parts of the world. We have many advisers, many people appointed by President Trump who are studying and evaluating what the purposes are that we are going to offer. We will probably know more about that in the coming months."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On multilateral organisations: "The administration, which is still in its first weeks, is evaluating how the United States will work in these international forums. At this moment, I therefore cannot say exactly in which forums we will participate and in which we will not, because it is still being decided by the administration. But it is important to stress that all the decisions the administration is taking, all the evaluations it is making on any subject, such as climate change or humanitarian assistance, it is always taking into account the interests of the United States."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On the 'change of partners' and Russia: "Both President Trump and Secretary of State Rubio are evaluating the position of the United States in the different conflicts and main issues that mark the present moment. Note that Secretary Rubio, in his first weeks of work, has already made many trips abroad, which is a sign of the importance this administration places on dialogue with different partners around the world." ; "I cannot comment on what may or may not change. We can only look at the actions, the meetings, the conversations that President Trump and Secretary Rubio are conducting now... On his first trip abroad, Secretary Rubio visited five Central American countries, highlighting the importance of working with the closest countries."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On the DRC: "The United States vehemently condemns the Rwanda-backed M23 offensive in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo and we call for the urgent protection of civilians. We call on all parties to return to the negotiating table and to reaffirm their commitments under the Luanda process. We urge M23 to withdraw from all controlled areas. We want peace and we call on all parties to seek that peace."

a6153.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a6153.name: Marco Rubio
a6153.title: US Secretary of State
a6153.speech: Condemned the attack on Goma perpetrated by M23. He and President Felix Tshisekedi [of the DRC] agreed on the importance of advancing the Luanda process. As Secretary Rubio has already said, the US position is to continue to call on all parties to return to the negotiating table and honour their commitments, towards a lasting peace in the region.

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On critical minerals deals: "We are still evaluating that type of agreement, involving metals and other resources. All of that is part of the strategy for Africa that the Trump administration is now developing... Africa is a continent with many important resources, including those essential for technology and for the future of the planet... Therefore, it is an area that we will continue to evaluate in these first months of this administration."

a6153.speaker: Amanda Roberson, US State Department official
a6153.name: Amanda Roberson
a6153.title: US State Department official
a6153.speech: On South Africa's land expropriation law and the G20: "On this law, it should be noted that Secretary Marco Rubio decided not to take part in the G20 meeting, because the administration does not agree with that law. In addition, as the Secretary himself indicated, the administration is not in favour of the main themes addressed at the G20. Among those themes is, for example, diversity, which is a theme that the Trump administration will not focus on. In short, Secretary Rubio assessed that the G20 and this meeting do not serve the interests of the United States." ; "Gender. That is a concept that the new administration does not support. There is a focus of the G20 on those issues, among others, which are no longer a priority of the United States, so it does not make sense for the Secretary to participate."

a6181.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6181.name: Volker Turk
a6181.title: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6181.speech: Said his office would need $500 million on top of its regular budget to help face towering rights challenges around the world this year: "Lives are at stake if we don't invest in human rights" ; speaking to country representatives at the United Nations in Geneva, he pointed to the vital work done by his staff in crisis-hit 2024 and warned that "in 2025, we expect no let-up in major challenges to human rights" ; "In this divided and polarised world, human rights assume even greater importance and must be one of the top priorities across the globe."

a6181.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6181.name: Volker Turk
a6181.title: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6181.speech: Said his office had raised the alarm over grave violations and abuses in a long line of places in 2024, from Gaza to Ukraine to Sudan and Myanmar; said his 2,000 staff members working across 92 countries had undertaken around 11,000 human rights monitoring missions and had observed nearly 1,000 trials; said the office's advocacy last year had contributed to the release of around 3,145 arbitrarily detained people; added that its staff had also documented some 15,000 situations of rights violations, supported more than 10,000 survivors of contemporary forms of slavery and more than 49,000 survivors of torture and their families.

a6181.speaker: Volker Turk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6181.name: Volker Turk
a6181.title: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a6181.speech: Said the office had requested the same $500 million amount last year but had received just $269 million of that, which was "four percent less than in 2023", adding that the office had been forced "to spend our reserves in order to make it through the year".

a6181.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a6181.name: Donald Trump
a6181.title: US President
a6181.speech: Said on returning to office last week that the United States - the world's largest foreign aid donor in dollar terms - would temporarily freeze almost all foreign aid pending a review.

a6181.speaker: Ravina Shamdasani, UN rights office spokeswoman
a6181.name: Ravina Shamdasani
a6181.title: UN rights office spokeswoman
a6181.speech: Told AFP on Thursday that the agency had received no information so far on US funding plans for 2025, "but we do of course remain hopeful that the US will continue its support".

a6181.speaker: Volker Turk (@volker_turk), post on X/Twitter, January 30, 2025
a6181.name: Volker Turk (@volker_turk)
a6181.title: post on X/Twitter, January 30, 2025
a6181.speech: "Our annual appeal is a call to action: human rights work must be funded - the cost of inaction is too high. As funds decline & needs rise, my Office is holding the line for humanity. But with less than 5% of the UN budget, we cannot do it alone. We need your help. Donate below."

a6181.speaker: A number of countries (country representatives at the event)
a6181.name: A number of countries (country representatives at the event)
a6181.speech: Voiced their support and vowed continued funding for the UN rights office during Thursday's event; the United States was not among them.

a6208.speaker: Ousmane Sonko, Prime Minister of Senegal
a6208.name: Ousmane Sonko
a6208.title: Prime Minister of Senegal
a6208.speech: Confirmed the freezing of a crucial $500 million financing package from the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC); “We cannot continue to depend on foreign aid,” he declared, acknowledging the fragility of the situation.

a6208.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a6208.name: Cyril Ramaphosa
a6208.title: President of South Africa
a6208.speech: Quickly defended the constitutionality of his approach on the land expropriation law, recalling that “we remain a democracy deeply rooted in the rule of law.”

a6208.speaker: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô, researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a6208.name: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô
a6208.title: researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a6208.speech: Said these decisions are part of a mercantilist strategy aimed at “optimising American spending”; “The Trump administration had clearly shown its hand during Donald’s first term by calling into question a great deal of spending and aid” ; “African countries did not anticipate Trump’s return and his unilateral policy” ; said the suspension could have “harmful” consequences “even once aid is restored.”

a6208.speaker: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô, researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a6208.name: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô
a6208.title: researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a6208.speech: “Another consequence would be the perception of the United States in Africa. China, its rival, has notably strengthened its image in certain African countries through its donations. Today, Trump’s decisions risk not only tarnishing the image of the United States but also giving China the opportunity to show that it is much more credible than its rival on certain policies,” he notes, stressing that “American interference policy is strengthening, with a militarisation of economic levers.”

a6208.speaker: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô, researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a6208.name: Dr Alioune Aboutalib Lô
a6208.title: researcher at the AKEM Centre in Istanbul
a6208.speech: Fears in particular reprisals against countries such as Senegal and Namibia, which have joined The Hague Group defending Palestinian rights.

a6216.speaker: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.name: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.speech: Recommended her removal from office based on its findings; in the opinion of the committee, the travel expenses which Justice Torkornoo “heaped on the Judicial Service when she travelled on holidays in September 2023, first to Tanzania with her husband and second, to the United States of America with her daughter, together with the payment of per diem to the spouse and daughter of the Chief Justice, constituted unlawful expenditure of public funds”, which it indicated cannot be justified in law or policy; those acts, it said, “constitute avoidable and reckless dissipation of public funds and, in the view of the committee, to have been occasioned by the overall head of the Judiciary and the Judicial Service, whose duty is to guard pubic resources allocated by the Government, is caught within the spectrum of stated misbehaviour.”

a6216.speaker: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.name: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.speech: Stated without fear or favour that the Chief Justice unjustifiably breached the provisions in article 295(a) and (b) of the Constitution, 1992, in the way and manner that she transferred one Mr Baiden, a staff of the Judicial Service, and said her conduct amounted to misbehaviour ; Indicated it was of the view that the conduct of Justice Torkornoo falls squarely in the category of conduct described as stated misbehaviour under article 146(1) of the Constitution, and that her action and conduct fell within the meaning and categories of stated misbehaviour as provided under article 146(1) of the Constitution, 1992.

a6216.speaker: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.name: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.speech: On the allegation of her request in a letter to former President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo for the appointment of more justices to the Supreme Court bench and her recommendation of certain names, said Justice Torkornoo cannot lay claim to ignorance of the nomination process and procedure, notwithstanding that the process is not spelt out in the Constitution but case law, noting that her own appointment as a Justice of the Supreme Court went through the very process set out in the Ghana Bar Association case: “Therefore, to seek, wittingly, to outwit this known process and procedure for appointing Supreme Court Justices amounts to misbehaviour in the eyes of the Committee and the Committee finds it as such.”

a6216.speaker: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.name: Committee of inquiry into the petitions against Chief Justice Torkornoo (report)
a6216.speech: Found, within a four-month period of hearing, that the grounds of stated misbehaviour under Article 146(1) had been established and recommended her removal from office.

a6216.speaker: President John Dramani Mahama (instrument of removal)
a6216.name: President John Dramani Mahama (instrument of removal)
a6216.speech: “Now therefore, know ye all men that I, John Dramani Mahama, President of the Republic of Ghana, in pursuance of the said Article 146 (9), do hereby REMOVE the said Chief Justice, Gertrude Araba Esaaba Sackey Torkornoo, from the office of Chief Justice and Justice of the Supreme Court, with effect from the date hereof. In witness whereof, I have hereunto set my hand caused the Presidential Seal to be affixed at Accra this 1st of Sept 2025.”

a6216.speaker: Presidency of Ghana (press statement, September 1, 2025)
a6216.name: Presidency of Ghana (press statement
a6216.title: September 1, 2025)
a6216.speech: Said the move was in accordance with Article 149 (9) of the 1992 Constitution: “President John Dramani Mahama has, in accordance with Article 146(9) of the 1992 Constitution, removed the Chief Justice, Her Ladyship Justice Gertrude Araba Esaaba Sackey Torkonoo, from office with immediate effect. This follows receipt of the report of the Committee constituted under Article 146(6) to inquire into a petition submitted by a Ghanaian citizen, Mr Daniel Ofori. After considering the petition and the evidence, the Committee found that the grounds of stated misbehaviour under Article 146(1) had been established and recommended her removal from office. Under Article 146(9), the President is required to act in accordance with the committee’s recommendation.”

a6216.speaker: Daniel Ofori, Ghanaian citizen (petition dated March 17, 2025)
a6216.name: Daniel Ofori
a6216.title: Ghanaian citizen (petition dated March 17, 2025)
a6216.speech: Petitioned the President to remove Justice Torkornoo from office on the grounds of misconduct and stated misbehaviour as Chief Justice.

a6216.speaker: 1992 Constitution of Ghana, Article 146(9)
a6216.name: 1992 Constitution of Ghana
a6216.title: Article 146(9)
a6216.speech: Stipulates that “The President shall, in each case, act in accordance with the recommendations of the committee.”

a6402.speaker: Barrick Gold Corporation quarter four 2024 results (released last week)
a6402.name: Barrick Gold Corporation quarter four 2024 results (released last week)
a6402.speech: The results indicate that the mine reported a 69 percent increase in net earnings to US$2.14 billion, a 51 percent increase in adjusted net earnings to US$2.21 billion, and a 30 percent rise in attributable EBITDA to US$5.19 billion for 2024 - the highest in over a decade; year-on-year operating cash flow increased by 20 percent to US$4.49 billion and free cash flow more than doubled to US$1.32 billion; a quarterly dividend of US$0.10 per share was maintained, bringing the total annual dividend to US$696 million, with a further US$498 million returned in buying back shares.

a6414.speaker: Felisberto Veiga, ACAISA (organisers of the "Sabores de Santiago" fair)
a6414.name: Felisberto Veiga
a6414.title: ACAISA (organisers of the "Sabores de Santiago" fair)
a6414.speech: "We have products, experiences and diversity, and we managed to show that flavours can be made in Santiago. And in partnership with the CEFP of Santa Catarina we managed to bring more than two dozen different flavours. That is why I believe it was a success" ; "The assessment of this experimental edition of the 'Sabores de Santiago' fair is positive. That is why I believe it was a success, above all because of the number of visitors and the fulfilment of the programme," he added, announcing that the event will be institutionalised and will have two editions a year, one around the Cinzas (Ash Wednesday) period and another in the summer.

a6470.speaker: HU Bin, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Djibouti (on the 21st and 22nd medical teams)
a6470.name: HU Bin
a6470.title: Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Djibouti (on the 21st and 22nd medical teams)
a6470.speech: Said the two teams rotated in May; that the 12 doctors of the 21st team, led by Dr Hou Wei, worked side by side with their Djiboutian colleagues to provide quality services to the local population, carried out health campaigns in the interior regions, donated a great deal of medical equipment and launched the first training course in traditional Chinese medicine, doing everything possible to contribute to the “basic medical coverage for the whole population” policy proposed by President Ismail Omar Guelleh and carried out by Health Minister Ahmed Robleh Abdilleh; said that last March, like their predecessors, they were decorated with a medal of the National Order of 27 June, “the highest form of appreciation and also a fine example of the renewed deepening of Sino-Djiboutian friendship” ; said the 22nd team, led by Dr Wu Lijuan, is made up of 12 people from 7 departments who immediately took up the intense work of Peltier Hospital, and that on International Children’s Day the embassy and the team jointly organised the activity “Warming the child’s heart, a joint China-Djibouti activity,” carrying out consultations and medical examinations for about a hundred children at the Daryel orphanage.

a6470.speaker: HU Bin, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Djibouti (on Chinese medical teams abroad)
a6470.name: HU Bin
a6470.title: Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Djibouti (on Chinese medical teams abroad)
a6470.speech: Said this year marks the 60th anniversary of the dispatch of Chinese medical teams abroad; that China is the only country in the world to have sent, free of charge and over such a long period, medical teams of this scale to other developing countries, reaching the five continents; that “one can say that this is the longest-running and most extensive international humanitarian aid in the world, unique in the history of human medical and health cooperation”; that since 1963 the Chinese government has sent a total of 30,000 doctors to 76 countries and regions, who have treated and cured 290 million patients; and that China sent doctors first to Africa, where most of its doctors also work, demonstrating the principles of “sincerity, real results, friendship and good faith” that China puts into practice in developing Sino-African relations.

a6470.speaker: Xi Jinping, President of China
a6470.name: Xi Jinping
a6470.title: President of China
a6470.speech: Summed up the spirit of the Chinese medical teams as “not fearing hardship, being ready to sacrifice, dedicated care for patients, great benevolence without limits” ; stressed that “the Chinese people love peace and cherish life, and the dispatch of Chinese medical teams abroad is a perfect illustration of this” ; stresses the need to place the Chinese people and their lives at the centre of the Chinese government’s concerns.

a6470.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a6470.name: Ismail Omar Guelleh
a6470.title: President of Djibouti
a6470.speech: Has stressed that the Republic of Djibouti has spared no effort since 1977 to improve its health system.

a6470.speaker: HU Bin, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Djibouti (on Sino-Djiboutian health cooperation)
a6470.name: HU Bin
a6470.title: Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Djibouti (on Sino-Djiboutian health cooperation)
a6470.speech: Said health is one of the most important and priority sectors in bilateral cooperation and summed it up in five features: the shared vision of the two heads of state of “placing the people and health at the centre of concerns,” which is the fundamental bedrock of health cooperation; the early start of the cooperation, with China sending a medical team to Djibouti in 1981, two years after diplomatic relations were established, when China itself had very limited resources; the diversity of forms of cooperation, including annual supplies of medicines and equipment, the Arta Regional Hospital operating since 2011 with a Chinese technical team still in service, the Tadjourah Hospital financed by China with work begun in 2022 to strengthen medical capacity in the north, and the 2014 “Journey of Clarity” project that cured 521 Djiboutian cataract patients; the diversity of participants, including two visits by the Chinese navy hospital ship Peace Ark holding free clinics for tens of thousands of inhabitants, the Hong Kong GX Foundation’s cataract-blindness elimination project launched in February 2023 with more than 400 operations by the end of March and a goal of restoring sight to 7,000 local patients within 5 years, and concrete cooperation by Chinese companies with Djibouti’s health department; and cooperation in times of crisis, with Djibouti donating one million US dollars to China during the pandemic’s peak there and China later providing large quantities of medical supplies, a team of medical experts and 1.4 million vaccine doses, Djibouti being the first country in East Africa to receive Chinese vaccines and China the first to supply vaccines to Djibouti bilaterally ; concluded that China will continue to work with Djibouti to strengthen cooperation in various fields, including health, to strengthen the long-standing friendship between the two peoples and open up finer prospects for the strategic partnership between the two countries.

a6507.speaker: Save the Children
a6507.name: Save the Children
a6507.speech: Said nearly half of children aged under five in Somalia could face acute malnutrition by mid-2026 due to a convergence of crises and as aid cuts reduce vital services that can stop malnutrition rates rising ; said this severe deterioration in malnutrition is compounded by global aid cuts reducing access to health and nutrition services, with insufficient vaccination coverage leading to an increase in diseases such as a current diphtheria outbreak ; said the closure of nutrition centres and health facilities—over a quarter of those supported by Save the Children—has left over 55,000 children without access to life-saving nutrition services since June.

a6507.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), global hunger monitor (new figures)
a6507.name: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC)
a6507.title: global hunger monitor (new figures)
a6507.speech: According to new figures from the IPC, flash flooding, below-average rainfall, high food prices, and ongoing conflict have combined to drive hunger levels up 30% across Somalia, with the south worst hit. The figures reveal that 4.4 million people, or just under a quarter of the population, are now expected to experience high levels of acute food insecurity by the end of 2025, including over 921,000 people facing emergency levels of food insecurity or Phase 4. The new data showed the number of children estimated to be suffering acute malnutrition could rise to 1.85 million children by July 2026, an increase of 9% from previous forecasts.

a6507.speaker: Binyam Gebru, Save the Children's Acting Country Director for Somalia
a6507.name: Binyam Gebru
a6507.title: Save the Children's Acting Country Director for Somalia
a6507.speech: “Somalia is embroiled in a protracted crisis, which is slowly grinding down the resilience of families and the wellbeing of children. Hunger – already at dire levels across Somalia - is on the rise, as climate shocks continue to wreak havoc, but it's even worse this year because now we are facing massive funding cuts which are already having severe impacts on children. We are already seeing more children arriving at our clinics in critical condition, and with fewer facilities open, many will have nowhere to turn. Not providing the funds that can help prevent extreme hunger is a political choice and one that needs to be reversed before it is too late for millions of children in Somalia.”

a6507.speaker: Save the Children
a6507.name: Save the Children
a6507.speech: Is calling on the international community and donors to urgently mobilize resources to restore and expand nutrition, health, and water services, warning that without immediate action the lives of hundreds of thousands of Somali children hang in the balance.

a6549.speaker: Gugu (not her real name), HIV-positive former sex worker and NGO project coordinator in Johannesburg
a6549.name: Gugu (not her real name)
a6549.title: HIV-positive former sex worker and NGO project coordinator in Johannesburg
a6549.speech: “I was one of the people who was able to get their medication in bulk. I usually collect a three-month prescription. But before my clinic closed, they gave me nine months’ worth of medication” ; “By then I already assumed that I was HIV-positive, and I told the nurse this” ; “We help pregnant sex workers get their ARVs, to ensure their children are born HIV-negative. We also do home visits to make sure that the mothers take their medication on time, and to look after their babies when they go for their monthly check-ups.”

a6549.speaker: Gugu (not her real name), HIV-positive former sex worker and NGO project coordinator in Johannesburg
a6549.name: Gugu (not her real name)
a6549.title: HIV-positive former sex worker and NGO project coordinator in Johannesburg
a6549.speech: Believes that many sex workers could be discouraged from going to public hospitals for their ARVs if they can no longer get them from clinics: “The problem with going to public hospitals is the time factor. In order to get serviced at these facilities, you have to arrive at 4 or 5am, and they may spend the whole day waiting for their medication. For sex workers, time is money” ; “The nurse who attended to us was very rude. She told us there was nothing special about sex workers” ; thinks this could lead to many sex workers defaulting on their medication, “especially because their hospital files contain a lot of personal information, and the concern is that sometimes the nurses at these local clinics aren’t always the most sensitive in dealing with this kind of information” ; “People don’t want to default on their ARVs. They’re scared that they’re going to die if they don’t get access to them” ; “I look after a nine-year-old. I want to live as long as I can to keep taking care of him. This isn’t just a problem for right now, we have to think about how it’s going to affect the next generation of women and young people.”

a6549.speaker: UNAids (report released on Thursday)
a6549.name: UNAids (report released on Thursday)
a6549.speech: Does not single out the US, but says that drastic cuts from a number of donors have sent shockwaves around the world and that the “phenomenal progress” in tackling the illness risks being reversed: “New HIV infections have been reduced by 40% since 2010, and 4.4 million children have been protected from acquiring HIV since 2000. More than 26 million lives have been saved”, warning that if the world does not act, there could be an extra six million new HIV infections and four million Aids-related deaths by 2029; said that, before the funding cuts, the annual numbers of new HIV infections and Aids-related deaths had sunk to their lowest levels in more than 30 years; according to UNAids, South Africa has about 7.7 million people living with HIV, the highest number in the world, about 5.9 million of them receiving antiretroviral treatment, resulting in a 66% decrease in Aids-related deaths since 2010.

a6549.speaker: George W Bush, then-US President
a6549.name: George W Bush
a6549.title: then-US President
a6549.speech: Launched an ambitious programme to combat HIV/Aids in 2003, saying it would serve the “strategic and moral interests” of the US.

a6549.speaker: South Africa’s government
a6549.name: South Africa’s government
a6549.speech: Says Pepfar funding contributed about 17% to its HIV/Aids programme, and that the money was used for various projects, including running mobile clinics to make it easier for patients to get treatment.

a6549.speaker: Prof Lynn Morris, Deputy Vice-Chancellor of Johannesburg’s Wits University
a6549.name: Prof Lynn Morris
a6549.title: Deputy Vice-Chancellor of Johannesburg’s Wits University
a6549.speech: “I think we’re going to start seeing an increase in the number of HIV infections, the number of TB cases, the number of other infectious diseases. And we’re going to start seeing a reversal of what was essentially a real success story. We were getting on top of some of these things” ; “There’s the long-term impact, which is that we’re not going to be getting new vaccines for HIV. We’re not going to be keeping on top of viruses that are circulating. Even with new viruses that might appear, we’re not going to have the surveillance infrastructure that we once had.”

a6549.speaker: Abdullah Ely, Associate Professor at Wits University
a6549.name: Abdullah Ely
a6549.title: Associate Professor at Wits University
a6549.speech: “We were developing a vaccine test to see how well that works, and then we would trial it on humans. The plan was to run the trials in Africa based on research carried out by Africans because we want that research to actually benefit our community as well as all mankind” ; “When the stop order came, it meant we had to stop everything. Only some of us have been able to get additional funding so we could continue our work. It’s set us back months, probably could even be a year” ; “That is a very big loss to South Africa and the continent. It means that any potential research that comes out of Africa will have to be tested in Europe, or the US.”

a6549.speaker: Universities (South Africa)
a6549.name: Universities (South Africa)
a6549.speech: In June, asked the government for a bailout of 4.6bn South African rand ($260m; £190m) over the next three years to cover some of the funding lost from the US.

a6549.speaker: Dr Phethiwe Matutu, head of Universities South Africa
a6549.name: Dr Phethiwe Matutu
a6549.title: head of Universities South Africa
a6549.speech: “We are pleading for support because South Africa is leading in HIV research, but it’s not leading for itself. This has ramifications on the practice and policies of the entire globe.”

a6549.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South Africa’s Health Minister
a6549.name: Aaron Motsoaledi
a6549.title: South Africa’s Health Minister
a6549.speech: Announced on Wednesday that some alternative funding for research had been secured: the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and the Wellcome Trust have agreed to donate 100m rand each with immediate effect, while the government would make available 400m rand over the next three years, bringing the total to 600m rand, way below the 4.6bn rand requested by researchers.

a6861.speaker: Tsegaye Yilma (PhD) and colleague, conference paper “Small Holder Irrigation and its Challenges in Ethiopia's Food Security Agenda: Lessons from Ghana”
a6861.name: Tsegaye Yilma (PhD) and colleague
a6861.title: conference paper “Small Holder Irrigation and its Challenges in Ethiopia's Food Security Agenda: Lessons from Ghana”
a6861.speech: The paper pointed out that Ethiopia’s irrigation schemes could not contribute to food security because they were small and focused on vegetable production; argued that for irrigation to contribute to Ethiopia's food security it needs to prioritise cereal production, and recommended investment in large-scale irrigation schemes which integrate smallholder farmers.

a6861.speaker: Food & Agriculture Organisation (FAO)
a6861.name: Food & Agriculture Organisation (FAO)
a6861.speech: According to the FAO, the year before 5.5 million tonnes of wheat were produced, and more than one million tonnes were imported at a cost of 431 million dollars.

a6861.speaker: US Department of Agriculture (statement quoted in a Bloomberg report of June 16, 2022)
a6861.name: US Department of Agriculture (statement quoted in a Bloomberg report of June 16
a6861.speech: Stated that Ethiopia's attempt to stop wheat imports by 2023 with “limited resources to adopt necessary technologies” is a “very unrealistic and unachievable target.”

a6861.speaker: Kansas State University research
a6861.name: Kansas State University research
a6861.speech: According to Kansas State University research, from 25pc to 30pc of the products from a wheat milling process are wheat by-products used for livestock consumption.

a7118.speaker: SADC (Southern African Development Community)
a7118.name: SADC (Southern African Development Community)
a7118.speech: Has called for bold action to reduce dependence on foreign aid and deepen regional integration, warning that unity and self-reliance are crucial to the bloc's future prosperity.

a7118.speaker: Elias Mpedi Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a7118.name: Elias Mpedi Magosi
a7118.title: SADC Executive Secretary
a7118.speech: Speaking at the SADC Council of Ministers meeting in Antananarivo, Madagascar, said shrinking foreign aid and global uncertainties should push the region to rely more on its own resources and markets: "We stand a better chance when we depend more on our own than on external support, which we have absolutely no control over," ; "This is a critical time for us to remain strong and focused on why we were established - to ensure peace, security and integration."

a7118.speaker: Elias Mpedi Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a7118.name: Elias Mpedi Magosi
a7118.title: SADC Executive Secretary
a7118.speech: Stressed that the region's economies cannot continue relying on exporting raw materials, saying the manufacturing sector's contribution to SADC's GDP is just 11%, far below the target of 30% by 2030; urged member states to speed up industrialisation, expand intra-regional trade, and remove barriers to the movement of goods and services: "If we continue exporting low-value goods, we will miss critical opportunities to modernise our manufacturing sector, create jobs, and fully benefit from our natural resources." ; also highlighted major energy projects underway to connect Angola, Malawi and Tanzania to the Southern African Power Pool by 2028, as well as efforts to launch pooled procurement of medicines to cut costs and improve health services.

a7118.speaker: Professor Amon Murwira, outgoing SADC Council of Ministers chairperson and Zimbabwe's minister of foreign affairs and international trade
a7118.name: Professor Amon Murwira
a7118.title: outgoing SADC Council of Ministers chairperson and Zimbabwe's minister of foreign affairs and international trade
a7118.speech: Echoed Magosi's call, saying the region must be driven by the vision of its founding fathers, a peaceful, secure, self-sufficient, and united community: "This was not a vision born out of convenience, but one driven by strategic foresight," ; "Let us remove any barriers amongst ourselves as we pursue regional integration for the prosperity and dignity of our people. Let us harmonise our systems and talk one language - the language of integration." ; urged other member states to follow Mauritius, Seychelles and Zimbabwe in allowing visa-free travel for SADC citizens, saying freer movement would strengthen unity ; noted that this year's theme captures the core priorities for the bloc's future and urged member states to take ownership of regional projects, harness natural resources, and "reduce reliance on external support."

a7118.speaker: Professor Amon Murwira, outgoing SADC Council of Ministers chairperson and Zimbabwe's minister of foreign affairs and international trade
a7118.name: Professor Amon Murwira
a7118.title: outgoing SADC Council of Ministers chairperson and Zimbabwe's minister of foreign affairs and international trade
a7118.speech: Warned that peace and security remain the foundation of economic progress, stressing the importance of collective action to resolve conflicts such as the crisis in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo: "An injury to one is an injury to us all. The threats to the peace we enjoy, if not contained, will undermine intra-SADC trade and the very fabric of our integration agenda."

a7118.speaker: Professor Amon Murwira, outgoing SADC Council of Ministers chairperson and Zimbabwe's minister of foreign affairs and international trade
a7118.name: Professor Amon Murwira
a7118.title: outgoing SADC Council of Ministers chairperson and Zimbabwe's minister of foreign affairs and international trade
a7118.speech: On the handover of the Council of Ministers chairmanship from Zimbabwe to Madagascar, assured the incoming chairperson of "Zimbabwe's full support" and urged all member states to work together to strengthen SADC: "Brick by brick and stone upon stone, we will continue building a stronger, united SADC that is a beacon of hope, stability, and progress."

a7118.speaker: Magosi and Murwira (both leaders)
a7118.name: Magosi and Murwira (both leaders)
a7118.speech: Both leaders emphasised that the slow signing and ratification of SADC protocols is a major stumbling block to progress; without timely ratification, they said, the region's ability to build a strong rules-based framework for development is weakened.

a7136.speaker: Abigail Kadirire, 42-year-old single mother-of-six and farmer in Kamutepe village, Rushinga, Zimbabwe
a7136.name: Abigail Kadirire
a7136.title: 42-year-old single mother-of-six and farmer in Kamutepe village, Rushinga, Zimbabwe
a7136.speech: "This is the second time this farming season that I am seeing it in my fields." ; "I sowed again in early January 2025 after struggling to get the seeds. Then fall armyworm came and ravaged my maize crops." ; "I thought this year I was going to have a good harvest, but it is now uncertain because of the pests."

a7136.speaker: Abigail Kadirire, farmer in Kamutepe village, Rushinga, Zimbabwe
a7136.name: Abigail Kadirire
a7136.title: farmer in Kamutepe village, Rushinga, Zimbabwe
a7136.speech: Said she is worried she may have to resort to food handouts again at a time when the future of aid funding is uncertain: "It is not easy to survive on handouts. But after the fall armyworm decreased yields on my maize crop this year, it appears I will survive on handouts again."

a7136.speaker: United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
a7136.name: United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
a7136.speech: According to the FAO, the armyworm, native to the Americas, was first detected in central and western Africa in early 2016, and within two years had spread across almost all of sub-Saharan Africa ; according to FAO, fall armyworm reduces maize yields by up to 73% and inflicts annual economic losses valued at $9.4 billion in Africa alone.

a7136.speaker: Patrice Talla, subregional coordinator for Southern Africa at the FAO and FAO representative in Eswatini, Lesotho and Zimbabwe
a7136.name: Patrice Talla
a7136.title: subregional coordinator for Southern Africa at the FAO and FAO representative in Eswatini, Lesotho and Zimbabwe
a7136.speech: "Climate change has contributed to outbreaks of migratory pests beyond their regions of origin, notably the fall armyworm." ; said more erratic rainfall and rising temperatures have created favourable conditions for the proliferation of various pests in Zimbabwe and throughout Africa ; "Global climate warming triggers an expansion of insect geographic coverage, increasing overwintering survival and the number of generations." ; "Reduced (maize) harvests result in lower incomes for affected households, compromising their capacity to buy food and other necessities."

a7136.speaker: Patrice Talla, subregional coordinator for Southern Africa at the FAO
a7136.name: Patrice Talla
a7136.title: subregional coordinator for Southern Africa at the FAO
a7136.speech: Said farmers could also use the Fall Armyworm Monitoring and Early Warning System (FAMEWS), a mobile app developed by the FAO to record data on fall armyworm through pheromone trap checks and field scouting.

a7136.speaker: Simbarashe Nyamasoka, acting deputy director in the Migratory Pests Control Department under Zimbabwe's Ministry of Lands
a7136.name: Simbarashe Nyamasoka
a7136.title: acting deputy director in the Migratory Pests Control Department under Zimbabwe's Ministry of Lands
a7136.speech: Said climate change has led to the prevalence of warm temperatures and wet condition, allowing pests to expand their geographical range: "Climate change has altered migratory patterns, allowing the armyworm to invade new areas more easily, potentially affecting agricultural regions that were previously less affected."

a7136.speaker: Simbarashe Nyamasoka, acting deputy director in the Migratory Pests Control Department under Zimbabwe's Ministry of Lands
a7136.name: Simbarashe Nyamasoka
a7136.title: acting deputy director in the Migratory Pests Control Department under Zimbabwe's Ministry of Lands
a7136.speech: Said climate-resilient agriculture, integrated pest management and regenerative agriculture are vital: "Adopting climate-smart agricultural practices such as drought-resistant crops, intercropping, and organic composting, promoting practices that enhance soil health and biodiversity... and combining biological, cultural, mechanical, and chemical methods helps manage the pests sustainably."

a7136.speaker: Simon Manguri, farmer from Kaidza village, Rushinga, Zimbabwe
a7136.name: Simon Manguri
a7136.title: farmer from Kaidza village, Rushinga, Zimbabwe
a7136.speech: Said his harvest this year would only be half of what he expected after fall armyworm infested his fields in January: "Farming is my only source of income. I sell surplus to the government earning money to feed, clothe and send my children to school."

a7136.speaker: Government of Zimbabwe (alerts via social media and radio)
a7136.name: Government of Zimbabwe (alerts via social media and radio)
a7136.speech: In January, the government sent alerts via social media and radios about the armyworm outbreak, providing information on control measures, including which pesticides to use.

a7136.speaker: Dr. Christian Thierfelder, principal cropping systems agronomist at CIMMYT
a7136.name: Dr. Christian Thierfelder
a7136.title: principal cropping systems agronomist at CIMMYT
a7136.speech: Said the environmental effect of pesticides was also a consideration so farmers were also exploring traditional practices like intercropping and multiple cropping: "And also the use of methods and practices ... like push-pull systems where you have legumes integrated with maize that repel fall armyworm."

a7136.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President
a7136.name: Donald Trump
a7136.title: U.S. President
a7136.speech: Announced a 90-day freeze on foreign aid in January.

a7196.speaker: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete, Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.name: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete
a7196.title: Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.speech: Wrote to express deep concerns regarding the impact of developmental cooperation and research collaborations between Namibia and European countries, particularly Germany, arguing that "These partnerships, while often presented as beneficial, have systematically compromised Namibia's economic freedom and independence. If we are truly committed to decolonising these collaborations and foreign aid structures, a fundamental shift is necessary."

a7196.speaker: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete, Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.name: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete
a7196.title: Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.speech: Reported that during her studies in Germany she encountered numerous injustices, and that colleagues, friends and relatives working within these partnerships have shared similar experiences of exploitation and discrimination; said the letter is inspired by the wisdom of the late Founding President Sam Nujoma, who firmly opposed injustice and fought for true liberation.

a7196.speaker: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete, Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.name: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete
a7196.title: Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.speech: Reported that in her PhD research on the commercialisation of non-timber forest products she found that the vast majority of profits are captured by European companies - mainly in Germany, France and Spain - as well as by Namibian exporters who, historically and in 2021, were all German-Namibians or white individuals, leading to severe income disparities and unfair compensation for indigenous producers; noted that in 2021 individual San harvesters received an average of only N$1 538, just 4% of the total value of the dried materials they traded, while five white exporters captured 17% and European companies took 79%, with Namibia's Devil's Claw exports estimated to be worth more than US$143 million annually.

a7196.speaker: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete, Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.name: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete
a7196.title: Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.speech: Argued that these injustices have persisted since colonial times despite BioTrade and Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) regulations funded by the German Development Agency since 1994, with no significant improvement in the livelihoods of indigenous harvesters; said that as a scholar who studied in Germany and worked on about two GIZ projects she has observed how exploitative these German-led initiatives are, continuing colonial-era practices through intellectual, strategic and systematic means rather than physical oppression, and that the bulk of the resources invested ultimately benefit German personnel and, to a lesser extent, German Namibians, while a handful of Namibian government officials who likely benefit corruptly remain silent.

a7196.speaker: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete, Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.name: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete
a7196.title: Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.speech: Called for a critical analysis of how much of German government funding through collaborative research, GIZ projects and Nama and Ovaherero genocide reparations truly reaches affected communities or national institutions, and argued that "our struggles are monetised, while so-called development projects serve as a facade to justify ongoing resource extraction and personnel financing."

a7196.speaker: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete, Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.name: Ndapewa Fenny Nakanyete
a7196.title: Namibian scholar (opinion piece author)
a7196.speech: Urged that Namibia "must significantly reduce or entirely sever reliance on development aid and collaborative research as forms of support from Germany", that GIZ's involvement in critical national sectors such as the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism should be reconsidered and strictly regulated, that universities must critically assess the true costs of collaborative research projects given the loss of Namibia's intellectual property rights, and that if she were president she would put projects like green hydrogen on hold pending a thorough assessment; concluded that "the decolonisation of development partnerships, foreign aid, and research collaborations is not just necessary - it is urgent."

a7398.speaker: Humanitarian agencies present in Baladweyne
a7398.name: Humanitarian agencies present in Baladweyne
a7398.speech: According to them, more than twenty people were killed in sudden floods in central Somalia, which affected a total of more than 460,000 people.

a7398.speaker: Local authorities (Baladweyne/Somalia)
a7398.name: Local authorities (Baladweyne/Somalia)
a7398.speech: Welcomed Djibouti's aid, stressing that this assistance is crucial to help those affected get back on their feet.
